claims.text: The review reports that most authorities place the extinction at about 445–443 million years ago.

The same section sets out three readings of how it unfolded: two main extinction pulses (the first at the base of the Hirnantian Stage, the second in its middle), a single more prolonged phase, or an additional earlier phase in the early Katian. The pulses are placed by rock layers, not by dates, so they are not drawn on the axis.

episodes.title: Frasnian–Famennian extinction (Late Devonian)
episodes.scope: This entry covers the Frasnian–Famennian event only. The later end-Devonian (Hangenberg) crisis is outside this check.

claims.text: A volcanic ash bed just below the Frasnian–Famennian boundary in Germany was dated to 372.360 ± 0.053 million years (2σ, measurement uncertainty only), so the boundary can be no older than 372.4 million years.
Combining that date with a published age model gives a boundary age of 371.93–371.78 million years (371.86 ± 0.08).
assumptions: the cited age model is correct
sedimentation was constant between the two Kellwasser horizons

claims.text: These values date the boundary, not the length of the extinction. How long the extinction lasted is not shown.
The authors place the onset of the mass extinction at 251.941 ± 0.037 million years ago, citing their earlier high-precision dating.
In each of the three sections studied, a large sulfur-isotope shift about 201.5 million years ago coincides with the level in the rock record that marks the extinction.
The Chicxulub impact in Yucatán is dated to 66.02 million years ago (no uncertainty given in the passage).
The extinction is placed at the dated impact because high-precision dating has established that the impact and the extinction were synchronous.
Wilf and colleagues (2023) call the impact the extinction's "unique cause".
Schulte and colleagues (2010), in a synthesis of rock records from around the world, concluded that the impact triggered the extinction.

Hull and colleagues (2020), using carbon-cycle models and past-temperature records, found support for the main Deccan gas release beginning and ending before the impact, with only the impact coinciding with the extinction.
Other studies examine what part was played by the Deccan Traps, a volcanic province in what is now India.
Schoene and colleagues (2019) dated the start of one pulse of eruptions to tens of thousands of years before the impact and the extinction.
They say their findings support models in which both events drove the environmental deterioration linked to the extinction.
O'Connor and colleagues (2024) note that the dating does not exclude Deccan volcanism as a contributing or primary cause.
Their own temperature records, from two sites in the western United States, suggest that on land volcanic climate change was not the primary cause.
This entry does not show how the extinction unfolded for each group of living things, or how long recovery took.

evidence.title: Space Radar Image of the Yucatan Impact Crater Site
Shaded Relief with Height as Color, Yucatan Peninsula, Mexico

evidence.locator: Abstract; Fig. 1 caption and the passage after it

opening.text: About 66 million years ago, a mass extinction marked the end of the Cretaceous Period.
An estimated three-quarters of species were lost, including every dinosaur that was not a bird.
At that time a large asteroid struck what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, forming the Chicxulub crater, now buried beneath younger rock.
Renne and colleagues (2013) reported dating that places the impact and the extinction within 32,000 years of each other.
That figure is a limit on how far apart the two could be, not a measured gap between them.
At two sites in the western United States, researchers identified the boundary by shock-altered minerals, an unusual enrichment in iridium, and the disappearance of fossil pollen and spores.

image.alt: Colour relief map of the north-west corner of the Yucatán Peninsula. A dashed semicircle labelled "Trough" curves inland from the coast. Arrows labelled "Cenotes (sinkholes)" point to small pits along it.
image.caption: Radar height map of the north-west Yucatán Peninsula, Mexico, with NASA's labels. The dashed line follows a shallow trough, 3 to 5 metres deep and about 5 kilometres wide, which NASA describes as a surface expression of the buried crater's outer boundary. Sinkholes (cenotes) are marked along it. Heights are greatly exaggerated. This is a rendering of elevation measurements, not a photograph of the crater. Data: Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, February 2000.
